articles.author: victormawira05-lgtm
articles.description:
What I Built


A safe production workflow for fixing slow time-series queries without ever touching prod.
The problem: Direct fixes on Postgres are risky. A bad index, a wrong type, or a long ALTER TABLE can lock production.
My solution: Fork / Fix / Delete using GitHub Copilot Agent Mode + Tiger Cloud MCP.
 FORK: Copilot called tiger_create_fork and cloned my live service db-63453 into db-63453-test (isolated, same data)
 FIX: Inside the fork, I reproduced the slow query. Used EXPLAIN ANALYZE, converted the table to a hypertable, fixed timestamp types to timestamptz, and added proper time-based indexes. Also used Tiger's Dump & Restore for migrating tables.
 DELETE: Verified with docs search via MCP, then ran tiger_delete_service — fork gone, prod untouched and still READY.
Who gets lazier? Any dev who is scared to touch prod DBs. The agent does the risky part in a sandbox.
Final state — proof of Delete:
db-63453 is READY in US East, 29 days trial left. The fork db-63453-test is gone. Only 1 service remains.

Monitoring after fix:
![monitoring]

Loom video: https://www.loom.com/share/48bb136113c14fa881559b259e4732c4
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/your-username/tiger-fork-fix-delete
Key files:
mcp.json — Tiger Cloud MCP + Docs MCP config
.github/copilot-instructions.md — Time-series best practices (hypertable, timestamptz, btree)
fix.sql — Before/After of slow query

sql
-- BEFORE: 2.3s sequential scan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT avg(value) FROM sensor_data WHERE time > now() - interval '1 day';

-- AFTER: 43ms index scan on hypertable
SELECT create_hypertable('sensor_data', 'time');
CREATE INDEX ON sensor_data (time DESC);

#postgres, #ai, #githubcopilot, #database
What's the worst production database incident you've ever accidentally caused, and how did you recover? Let me know in the comments below!
articles.title: Fork, Fix, Delete: Safe Database Migrations with GitHub Copilot and Tiger Cloud

articles.author: Bruno Haible
articles.description:
GNU coreutils or uutils coreutils? Ubuntu 26.04 ships with both. I prefer to use the GNU coreutils, for several reasons:
The uutils are written in Rust and therefore make use of the Rust/Cargo modules. This is an ecosystem of small modules, each written by a different author and sometimes maintained, but more often unmaintained over longer time. This ecosystem is vulnerable to the same kinds of supply chain attacks as we have seen in the npm world, where packages are occasionally taken over by malicious people (either because the maintainer behaves in an irresponsible way, or by takeover via stolen credentials, or by domain name squatting, etc.). I cannot trust a package that relies on 100 or more such modules.
The uutils people are fighting the GPL, by putting their code under the MIT lic…

articles.author: Suresh Kumar Pallapothu
articles.description:
Containers are ephemeral. When a Pod crashes or Kubernetes moves it, everything on its local disk is gone. For a web server that is fine. For AI it is costly: vector indices take time to rebuild, and model weights are many gigabytes that you do not want to download again every restart.
In plain terms: A container's disk is a whiteboard that gets wiped whenever the room is reassigned. A persistent volume is a filing cabinet in the corridor that every new room can open.
Diagram: A container's local filesystem is discarded when its Pod crashes or is rescheduled. Vector indices and multi-gigabyte model weights must outlive the Pod, so they need persistent volumes. See the animated version.
Kubernetes separates the storage from the application with two resources.

articles.author: VANSH ARORA
articles.description:
When building a local-first repository intelligence engine, speed is everything. A cold build on a 100k-file benchmark can take 45 to 55 seconds. But during active coding, developers expect instantaneous updates when saving a file.
In TokenCap, we implemented an atomic sharded incremental cache in src/incremental/cacheManager.js.
Atomic Sharding: Instead of a monolithic cache file, intelligence graphs are sharded into modular JSON blocks keyed by file path hashes.
Content-Based Checksums: Cache validity is verified via SHA-256 checksums rather than volatile filesystem mtimes.
Version Guard: Any version mismatch between the running TokenCap binary and stored cache forces an automatic, safe cold rebuild instead of mis-reading stale schemas.
Scoped Invalidation: When src/auth.js changes, TokenCap only re-parses auth.js and updates direct incoming and outgoing graph edges.
On our benchmark repository of 1,200 files:
Cold Build (Zero Cache): 1.14s
Warm Full Rebuild: 290ms
Scoped Incremental Build (1 File Edit): 57ms




# Watch mode with sub-60ms incremental rebuilds
tokencap make --watch

Output:
Watching for changes (rebuild after 300ms idle)...
✓ Change detected in src/auth/jwt.js
✓ Invalidation scope: 1 file, 4 affected callers
✓ Rebuilt incremental snapshot in 57ms (.tokencap/snapshot.md)

Because rebuilds take under 60ms, the VS Code extension auto-captures on save without interrupting typing cadence.
Explore the caching implementation at tokencap.vansharora.app
articles.title: How We Built an Atomic, Sharded Incremental Cache with 57ms Rebuild Times
